Keywords: regression test, failing test, reproduce bug test, bug fix test
Description: Write a test that fails because of the bug before fixing it.
How to Apply: Encode the repro as a test; run it and watch it fail for the right reason; fix; watch it pass; keep it.
Pitfalls: A test written after the fix that never failed and may not test the bug.

Keywords: tdd, test driven, red green refactor, test first, unit test
Description: Write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest code, then refactor.
When to Use: New behavior with clear inputs and outputs.
How to Apply: Red: one small failing test. Green: minimal code to pass. Refactor: clean up with tests green. Repeat.
Pitfalls: Tests coupled to implementation details; skipping the refactor step.

Keywords: acceptance test, given when then, bdd, end to end, user story, criteria
Description: Tests that express acceptance criteria in user terms.
How to Apply: One test per criterion: Given a state, When an action, Then an observable outcome; run through the public interface.
Pitfalls: Too many slow end-to-end tests; testing UI details instead of behavior.

Keywords: characterization, golden master, legacy, pin behavior, approval test
Description: Tests that record what the code does today, right or wrong, so refactoring cannot change it unnoticed.
When to Use: Refactoring or migrating code with weak test coverage.
How to Apply: Call the code with representative inputs; assert on the current outputs; cover branches you will touch; then refactor.
Pitfalls: Treating recorded wrong behavior as correct forever without flagging it.

Keywords: property based, hypothesis, quickcheck, fuzz, invariant, generative
Description: Assert properties that hold for all inputs and let a generator search for counterexamples.
When to Use: Parsers, serializers, algorithms and anything with clear invariants.
How to Apply: State an invariant (round trip, ordering, idempotence); generate inputs; shrink failures to a minimal case; keep found cases as regression tests.
Pitfalls: Properties that just restate the implementation.

Keywords: contract test, api contract, consumer driven, pact, schema validation, integration
Description: Verify that a provider and its consumers agree on the interface.
When to Use: Services and modules that talk across an API or message boundary.
How to Apply: Capture the requests and responses consumers rely on; run them against the provider in CI; fail on breaking changes.
Pitfalls: Contracts that drift from real usage.

Keywords: snapshot, golden file, approval, output comparison
Description: Compare output with a stored reviewed version.
When to Use: Rendered output, generated code, large structured responses.
How to Apply: Store the expected output; diff on each run; review and approve intentional changes explicitly.
Pitfalls: Updating snapshots blindly whenever they fail.

Keywords: benchmark, load test, performance test, latency test, k6, jmeter, locust, microbenchmark
Description: Measure performance repeatably against a baseline.
When to Use: Performance work and changes on hot paths.
How to Apply: Fix the workload, data and environment; warm up; run several times; report median and tail (p95/p99); compare against the baseline.
Pitfalls: Single noisy runs; benchmarks on a laptop compared with production.

Keywords: hermetic, isolated, deterministic, no network, test isolation, fixtures, fake clock
Description: Tests that depend on nothing outside themselves: no shared state, network, real clock or order.
When to Use: Flaky tests and any test touching time, randomness, files or network.
How to Apply: Create and clean up fixtures per test; inject clock and random seed; fake network calls; run tests in random order.
Pitfalls: Hidden global state such as singletons, environment variables and caches.

Keywords: test pyramid, unit integration e2e, test strategy, coverage balance
Description: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests.
When to Use: Planning or reviewing the tests for a change.
How to Apply: Test logic at the lowest level that can see the behavior; add integration tests for boundaries; keep end-to-end tests for critical journeys.
Pitfalls: An ice-cream cone: mostly slow end-to-end tests.
